chef.intro: Learn professional cooking from technique to kitchen management. Master the methods that turn ingredients into dishes, and the leadership that runs a kitchen under pressure.

skillDomains.name: Cooking Technique
skillDomains.description: The foundational methods every chef must master.

skills.name: Heat Methods
skills.description: Dry heat, moist heat, and combination methods.

modules.title: The three families of cooking
modules.content:
Dry heat

Roasting, grilling, frying, sautéing. Produces browning and concentrated flavour.

Moist heat

Boiling, steaming, poaching, braising. Tenderises and preserves moisture.

Combination

Braising, stewing. Starts with dry heat (browning) then adds liquid.

The rule

Match the method to the ingredient. A tender cut of beef is best dry-heated. A tough cut needs moist heat and time.

modules.title: Browning — the flavour maker
modules.content:
The Maillard reaction is the chemical process that browns food and creates complex flavours. It happens above 140°C.

How to brown well

  • Dry the surface — wet food steams instead of browning
  • Hot pan, room-temperature food — cold food cools the pan
  • Don't crowd the pan — crowded food steams
  • Wait before flipping — browning takes time
  • Season after — salt draws moisture to the surface

Browning is 80% of the flavour in most meat dishes.

steps.q: You're cooking a tough cut of beef (chuck). Which method?
o: Braise (dry heat then moist, long cook)
steps.f: Tough cuts need long moist heat to break down collagen.

steps.q: You want a steak with a crisp crust and juicy inside. Which method?
steps.f: Searing creates the crust and Maillard flavour.

steps.q: The chicken in your pan is steaming, not browning. What's wrong?
o: Too crowded or the chicken is wet
steps.f: Crowded or wet food steams. Dry it and give it space.

skills.name: Seasoning & Flavour
skills.description: The balance that turns cooking into cooking well.

modules.title: The five tastes and balance
modules.content:
Every dish is a balance of five tastes:

  • Salty — salt, soy, fish sauce
  • Sour — lemon, vinegar, tamarind
  • Sweet — sugar, honey, ripe vegetables
  • Bitter — greens, coffee, char
  • Umami — savoury, from glutamate-rich ingredients like tomatoes, mushrooms, fermented sauces

The rule

Taste as you cook. When something is flat, it usually needs salt or acid. When it's harsh, it usually needs fat or sugar.

modules.title: Seasoning in layers
modules.content:
Great chefs season at every stage, not just at the end.

Layers of seasoning

  1. Marinade — penetrate the protein before cooking
  2. During cooking — salt the water for pasta, season the vegetables as they sauté
  3. Finishing — flaky salt, a squeeze of lemon, fresh herbs

Why layers matter

A dish seasoned only at the end tastes salty on the surface and bland inside. Layers distribute seasoning through the dish.

steps.q: A soup tastes flat. What do you add?
steps.f: Flat usually means under-salted or lacking acid.

steps.q: A stew tastes harsh and acidic. What do you add?
o: Fat (butter, cream, oil) or a bit of sugar
steps.f: Fat and sugar round off harsh flavours.

steps.q: A sauce tastes thin. What do you do?
o: Reduce it and finish with butter or starch
steps.f: Reduction concentrates flavour. Finishing with butter (monter au beurre) adds body.

skillDomains.name: Menu Design
skillDomains.description: Building a menu that works for the kitchen and sells.

skills.name: Menu Planning
skills.description: Design a menu customers want and the kitchen can deliver.

modules.title: What makes a good menu
modules.content:
The two audiences

  • Customers — want dishes that sound appealing, priced fairly, and arrive hot
  • The kitchen — needs a menu that can be executed consistently under pressure

Balance

  • Not too many dishes (12-16 mains is plenty)
  • Categories: starters, mains, sides, desserts
  • Each category has variety: light/heavy, meat/vegetarian
  • Seasonal — use what's fresh and cheap
  • Price spread — a few high, most middle, a couple low

The rule

Every dish must earn its place. If it doesn't sell, cut it. If it's too slow to prepare, rethink it.

modules.title: Design a restaurant menu
modules.prompt: A new restaurant wants to open in your city, serving contemporary West African food. Design a menu for lunch service. Include 3 starters, 4 mains, 2 sides, and 2 desserts. Justify your choices.
modules.context: Menus are commercial documents. Every dish must work for the kitchen and the customer.
rubric: Total of 11 dishes — not too many for a small kitchen
Uses West African ingredients and techniques
Includes at least one vegetarian main
Includes dishes that share prep work with others
Prices range from mid-range to premium
Justifies dishes based on customer appeal and kitchen practicality

skills.name: Kitchen Brigade
skills.description: The roles and the flow during service.

modules.title: Classic kitchen roles
modules.content:
The brigade de cuisine

  • Executive chef — runs the whole kitchen operation
  • Head chef / chef de cuisine — runs the line during service
  • Sous chef — second in command, fills in everywhere
  • Chef de partie — runs a specific station (grill, sauce, veg, fish)
  • Commis — junior chef, learning the stations
  • Plongeur — dish washer and prep assistant

Small kitchens

Most West African kitchens don't have this many roles. But the principle of station-based work and clear hierarchy applies.

steps.q: During a busy dinner service, who calls the orders?
steps.f: The head chef calls orders and coordinates timing. Single point of control.

steps.q: One station is falling behind. What do you do?
o: Reassign staff or slow the incoming orders
steps.f: Reassign or slow the pace. Never let one station fail the whole service.

steps.q: The quality check before a dish leaves the pass is the job of:
steps.f: The pass is the last chance to catch a mistake. The head chef owns it.

skills.name: Food Cost
skills.description: The number that makes or breaks a restaurant.

modules.title: The food cost percentage
modules.content:
Food cost % = (Cost of ingredients ÷ Selling price) × 100

Typical targets

  • Full-service restaurant: 28-35%
  • Fast casual: 25-30%
  • Fine dining: 30-40%

Why it matters

Food cost above 35% usually means either low prices or waste. Both kill profit.

How to control it

  • Accurate costing for every dish
  • Regular inventory
  • Portion control
  • Reduce waste (use trim, make stocks)
  • Adjust prices when ingredient costs rise

steps.q: A dish costs 2,000 Le to make and sells for 6,000 Le. Food cost %?
A dish costs 3,000 Le to make and sells for 5,000 Le. Food cost %?
steps.f: 3,000 ÷ 5,000 × 100 = 60%. Way too high. Either raise the price or reduce the cost.

steps.q: Chicken prices rise 20%. Your main dish uses chicken. What do you do?
o: Adjust the price or portion to keep food cost in range
steps.f: Adjust to protect the food cost %. Silent losses add up.

modules.title: Build a dish costing sheet
modules.prompt: Design a costing sheet for every dish on a menu. It should include ingredients, quantities, unit costs, total cost, target price, and food cost %.
steps: List every ingredient and its cost
Calculate total ingredient cost per portion
Calculate the price that meets the target
Compare to what you'd actually charge

skillDomains.name: Leadership
skillDomains.description: The kitchen is a team. Leading it is a skill.

skills.name: Managing the Team
skills.description: Get the best from people under pressure.

modules.title: Kitchen leadership
modules.content:
Professional kitchens are high-pressure, hot, and fast. Bad leadership destroys teams. Good leadership builds them.

What works

  • Clear expectations — everyone knows their station and standards
  • Consistency — same standards on quiet and busy nights
  • Calm under pressure — panic spreads; so does calm
  • Correction in private, praise in public
  • Teach, don't just criticise

What doesn't

  • Shouting and insults (the old-school approach — proven to fail)
  • Inconsistency
  • Blaming others when things go wrong
  • Ignoring problems until they explode

steps.q: A commis chef makes the same mistake three times. What do you do?
o: Take them aside, show the correct technique, watch them practice
steps.f: Correct the technique, not the person. Show, then watch, then correct again if needed.

steps.q: During a busy service, the sous chef is panicking. What do you do?
o: Stay calm, slow the incoming orders, reassign as needed
steps.f: Calm is contagious. Slow the pace, reassign stations.

steps.q: A team member is consistently late. What do you do?
o: Address it privately — is there a problem? Can you help?
steps.f: Address it privately. Latent problems become bigger problems. Ask, then act.
